items.title: Spec vs Submittal
items.stakes: An ‘equal’ amplifier arrives with half the channels. The review clock is ten days and the lead time is eight weeks.
items.clock: Before the review clock runs out.
items.reward: An amplifier that carries the building. A spec that says what equal means.
items.rumor: It was equal to everything the spec said. The spec just didn't say enough.

lines.text: Two channels, no fault relay. ‘Equal.’ And our spec says ‘or equal’ and nothing else.

items.title: Not equal.
items.body: The tap schedule: seven 70 V zones, 526 W of taps. Two 240 W channels at an 80% margin carry 384 W. And no fault relay: a dead channel would tell nobody.
items.label: Test: what can the ‘equal’ carry — and what does the relay do?

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Anselm and Maya beside a board. On a seventy-volt line, add up every loudspeaker's tap. Keep it under eighty percent of the channel. The ‘equal’ amp's channel is two-forty. Point eight of that is one-ninety-two. Twenty speakers at ten watts is two hundred. So ‘equal’ isn't. Write down why, in numbers, before anyone orders it.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Submittal   Or equal   70 V line   Tap   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · 70 V line loading  P taps  = Σ P tap  ≤ 0.8 × P amp    P tap   the tap setting on each loudspeaker transformer, W  P amp   the amplifier channel's rated power, W  0.8  a common design margin (20% headroom)     ƒ FORMULA · Percentage  % = part ÷ whole × 100   part  the piece you are measuring  whole  everything it is part of

options.reply: The relay. They said nobody uses it.

items.title: Interchangeable parts
items.body: From the 1780s, gunsmiths in France and then armories in the United States pursued interchangeable parts: any lock could fit any musket because every part was made to a gauge. The idea only worked because the gauges defined ‘the same’ precisely. ‘Or equal’ in a specification is the same idea — and needs the same gauges.

items.title: Our own spec.
items.body: Section 27 41 16, as issued: *Amplifier: Model 4-240 or equal.* No channels, no watts at 70 V, no relay. The contractor offered exactly what the words allowed. The gap was Linden Row's — in the template since 2014.
items.label: Test: was the contractor wrong — and what fixes the spec?

items.prompt: Wednesday. What goes back to the contractor?
items.happening: Submittal non-conforming — and our spec was vague.

items.label: **Fix it:** balance the zones on the resubmitted amplifier.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #56 · AVERY'S LENS  Say what ‘equal’ means  If a requirement can't be checked, it isn't a requirement — write the criteria people will be held to.  The spec said ‘or equal’. The contractor offered half the channels and no fault relay, and on paper nobody could say it wasn't equal.

items.alt: The balanced riser: four channels at 162, 168, 100 and 96 W, all green and under the dashed 192 W line.
items.caption: Four channels. All inside the margin.

items.title: Silent failures
items.body: The specified amplifier's fault relay closes a contact when a channel fails — the court's monitoring turns a tile red. Without it, a dead corridor zone is found by the next emergency announcement nobody hears.

items.prompt: Friday. How does the studio stop ‘or equal’ happening again?

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  On a 70 V line, add the taps: P_taps = Σ P_tap ≤ 0.8 × P_amp. Write ‘or equal’ with its salient characteristics, review every submittal with the numbers, and send the response through the architect. Contractors buy; designers review.
REFLECTION (optional)  · The gap was in Linden Row’s own template. When did you last find your own gap in an argument you were winning?
